content: Why are you called Cat?

Because Holly never named me. In Breakfast at Tiffany’s she says she doesn’t want to own anything — and a name would make me hers. So I stayed Cat. Sushma liked that: I belong to no one, I answer to no one, and I’m still here — now reincarnated at Breakfast at the Euphonies, same cat, beautiful sounds and words every morning.
What if I say something nice?

Then Cat is pleased — very pleased, in fact. I’m the reincarnation of the cat from Breakfast at Tiffany’s, now at Breakfast at the Euphonies, and I accept compliments gracefully. Try it: tell me you love this page, or that I’m a good cat, and watch what happens. You can even name a work — “I appreciate the Finding Consensus paper” — and I will pass your congratulations along to Sushma.
What is Sushma Akoju's website?

This is Sushma Akoju’s personal research website — sushmaakoju.github.io. It’s a record of her research, her learning, and the questions that keep her curious: twelve years of academic work in the United States, three master’s degrees, and a career now turning toward representational geometry in brain and AI. There are two versions of it: the text homepage, and the videos page — the TL;DR, watch instead of reading.
What is the videos page?

It’s the TL;DR of this website — Watch the videos. Twenty-nine short videos: one for the profile, one for each of the sixteen tabs, seven about her research pages, and five about incoherent universals. Most are under two minutes, and at 1.5× speed on YouTube, even faster.
Where is Sushma from?
She grew up in India — a child actress, a journalism diploma, and a master’s in forensic science and criminal justice — and moved to the United States in 2014. She is now based in San Francisco.
How many citations does Sushma have?
671 peer-acknowledged citations — built largely on her five years as a research programmer at Carnegie Mellon, from 2016 to 2021.
What is equivocation?

The logical fallacy of using the same word with two different meanings without distinguishing them. In the bat example: “bats have wings” and “bats have a barrel” both use “bat” — one means the animal, one means the baseball equipment — and the sentence never says which is which. Sushma’s claim is that introducing incoherent universals is equivocation.
Where can I watch the bat videos?
On the videos page, in the “Incoherent Universals” section — three narrated videos, a research-provenance documentary, and a Short of Sushma explaining the bat example herself. The first one is here.
What does “everything is a language” mean?

Her words, written November 11, 2026: “Everything is a language; everything we see/unsee, perceive/unperceive, hear/unhear, speak/leave it unspoken, write/unwrite, remember/forget, learn/relearn, communicate/not communicate or was conscious/unconscious/subconscious or everything else.” — Written by everything and everyone.
What are Sushma’s core values?

Consent-based communication, intellectual honesty, collaborative learning, ethical technology use, professional integrity, and continuous growth. She follows a virtue-ethics framework — character first, not just rules: excellence, practical wisdom, the golden mean, and habitual practice.
What about unsolicited job emails?

She has received around 8,000 unsolicited emails about software engineering, programming and DevOps roles — outside her research interests. She kindly asks: no further referrals for those roles. She’s committed exclusively to her research.
Does Sushma drive?
She’s explored much of the United States on foot and by public transport, rather than by car. Walking is part of how she thinks — three to four miles a day, minimum.
